newsitem.title: USA: Mastercard sues to stop Advanta-Amex rewards program.
newsitem.headline: Mastercard sues to stop Advanta-Amex rewards program.

text.p: Mastercard International said Tuesday it was suing Advanta Corp. and American Express for allowing MasterCard holders to earn points that can be redeemed in Amex's rival awards programme.
The lawsuit, filed Monday in the U.S. District Court in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, follows a similar suit by Visa U.S.A. against American Express in late November.

The no-fee credit card, called the Rewards Accelerator Card, enables American Express cardmembers enrolled in its Membership Rewards programme to earn additional points for purchases made with Visa or Mastercards issued by Advanta.
Launched in early November, it is the first such card alliance between American Express, which is based in New York, and an issuer of another card in the United States.
Both lawsuits seek an injunction to force American Express and Horsham, Pa.-based Advanta to discontinue the Rewards Accelerator programme.
MasterCard's suit alleges trademark infringement, unfair competition, breach of contract and interference with contractual relations.
"While we regret that we had to take legal action against a long-standing MasterCard member, we were left with little choice," said Alan Heuer, MasterCard U.S. Region president.
"Frankly, we're surprised that, as a member of MasterCard, Advanta would misuse the MasterCard trademark and inappropriately link it with a competitive programme," he said.

MasterCard asserts that the Rewards Accelerator programme promotes American Express products by misusing the MasterCard trademark, creating a "false impression" that MasterCard is a participant in the American Express Rewards Programme.
The programme seeks to link usage of MasterCard cards, issued by Advanta, to American Express Membership Rewards, thus promoting American Express card membership, it said.

Heuer said the programme created a strong likelihood of confusion among consumers and diluted the MasterCard trademark. MasterCard licenses its 13,000 member financial institutions in the United States to use the MasterCard mark to promote its card programmes.

Visa has said its suit seeks to stop American Express from taking a "free ride" on the Visa brand through the programme with Advanta. It has requested that Advanta terminate the programme and cease soliciting cardholders.
An American Express spokeswoman said the Mastercard suit "has no merit." She said Visa and Mastercard dominate the market and attempt to prevent members from developing new products.

Earlier this year, American Express Chairman and CEO Harvey Golub personally asked bankers to consider issuing American Express cards. The Visa and Mastercard associations promptly criticised Golub's proposal as an attempt to divide the membership of the groups.

Robert McKinley, president of RAM Research Group, which tracks the credit card industry, said the dispute achieves American Express' objectives by bringing the issue of competition in the card industry into the spotlight.
"American Express is not going to lose anything," McKinley said. "I think they're gloating over this." He noted that the Department of Justice is looking into industry practices.
McKinley said that while it is difficult to predict the outcome of the litigation, "those with the most to lose are Visa and Mastercard."

Advanta said in a statement that it reached a "standstill" agreement with Visa. But an Advanta spokeswoman declined to say if that meant Advanta was no longer soliciting business for Rewards Accelerator cards tied to the Visa network.

"In order to facilitate an orderly hearing and resolution of the preliminary injunction issues by Jan. 22, 1997, the parties have agreed to a standstill agreement on both sides without prejudice to either side's rights," the statement said.
Advanta's stock fell $1 to $43.25 on Nasdaq. American Express fell $1 to $50.875 on the New York Stock Exchange.
